items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a speech introduction?

options.label: To gain attention and preview the topic
To thank everyone who helped you prepare the talk
To answer all questions before they are asked
To list every detail the audience should remember

items.explanation: Introductions capture attention and preview the topic.

items.prompt: What does the term 'eye contact' mean in public speaking?

options.label: Staring steadily at one friendly person for the whole talk
Reading your notes without looking up at the room
Looking at the back wall above everyone's heads
Looking at different audience members while speaking

items.explanation: Eye contact means looking at various listeners to connect.

options.label: A deliberate short silence between ideas
A slower speaking speed kept up throughout a talk
A mistake where you lose your place and forget words
A filler sound such as 'um' used to fill silence

items.explanation: A pause is a deliberate silence used for emphasis or clarity.

items.prompt: Why should a speaker adapt the language to the audience?

options.label: So the speaker can get away with using fewer examples
So listeners can follow and relate to the message
So the talk can be made as short as possible
So the speaker can show off specialist words

items.explanation: Adapting language helps the audience understand.

items.prompt: A speaker's hands shake before a talk. Which explanation of this is most accurate?

options.label: It will get worse if the speaker breathes slowly and deeply beforehand
It shows the speaker has not prepared enough and will likely struggle
It means the speaker is too anxious to deliver the talk well
It is a normal body response to nerves that can be managed

items.explanation: Shaking is a common stress response and manageable.

items.prompt: A new employee fills each slide with full paragraphs and reads them aloud word for word. After a few minutes, most of the audience is looking at their phones. Which explanation best accounts for the loss of attention?

options.label: Text-heavy slides compete with the speaker's voice for attention, so the audience gives up on the visuals
Listeners read faster than the speaker talks, so the speaker adds little and attention drifts
Reading from the slides makes the speaker's voice quieter and flatter, so listeners struggle to hear the points
Long paragraphs are too hard to understand when presented aloud, so the audience cannot follow the content

items.explanation: When the speaker only repeats on-screen text, listeners read ahead and have no reason to listen.

items.prompt: You have exactly 5 minutes for a talk with an opening, three main points and a close. Which plan uses the full five minutes?

options.label: Opening 30 seconds, three points of 1 min 20 seconds each, close 30 seconds
Opening 15 seconds, three points of 2 minutes each, close 15 seconds
Opening 1 min, three points of 2 minutes each, close 1 min
Opening 1 min, three points of 1 min each, close 30 seconds

items.prompt: A slide holds a 60-word paragraph about Q3 sales growth. Which revision best applies the rule that slides support rather than repeat the speaker?

options.label: Keep the full paragraph on the slide and read it slowly, so that the audience gets every detail
Show "Sales grew 12% in Q3" with one simple chart, and say the detail aloud
Keep the paragraph but bold the main numbers, so the audience can spot the key figures in it
Shrink the font so the paragraph fits, then turn each sentence of it into a bullet point

items.explanation: A headline and one visual with spoken detail lets the slide support the talk.

items.prompt: Your hands shake before a talk begins and your breathing is shallow. You have two minutes. Which action best applies a nerve-management technique?

options.label: Drink a large coffee so you feel more alert and energetic when you begin speaking
Breathe slowly with a longer exhale, then plant your feet and open with your first line
Tell yourself firmly to stop being nervous, since suppressing the feeling makes the shaking fade
Reread all your notes quickly to make sure you have not forgotten anything in the talk

items.explanation: Slow exhale breathing lowers arousal and a rehearsed opening gives a stable start.

items.prompt: A speaker's delivery of a rehearsed talk sounds flat. Recording shows steady pace, same pitch, and no pauses, while the content is strong. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: The speaker is reciting memorised wording instead of thinking through the ideas
The speaker is gesturing so much that attention is split and the voice stays level
The content is too complex, so the speaker has no spare attention for vocal variety
The speaker has chosen the wrong topic for the audience's interests and feels disengaged

items.explanation: Monotone, steady pacing with no pauses typically signals recitation of memorised text.

items.prompt: The same 10-minute talk got strong engagement with a local team in person but weak engagement on a video call with the same people. Which comparison best explains the difference?

options.label: Online, the talk ran shorter than planned, so people had too little time to engage with it
Online listeners process spoken content less well, so the talk needed simpler wording and less detail
In person, the room's energy carries the talk, so the online version only needed more slides
Online, the speaker lost audience cues and visual variety, so pacing and interaction did not adapt

items.explanation: Virtual settings reduce feedback cues, so the speaker must adapt pacing and add interaction.

items.prompt: A presenter walks through a dense results table at a fast, even pace with no pauses. Listeners later say they 'followed the words but lost the numbers.' Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The table font was too small to read from the back, so the audience could not take in the figures and enlarging it would have fixed the problem
Her pronunciation of the figures was unclear, so listeners misheard several digits and could not hold on to the values she read aloud to them
Her hand gestures competed with the figures for attention, so listeners watched her hands instead of listening to the values she was reading
Dense new data needs processing time, and without pauses or signposting listeners could not link the figures to their meaning

items.explanation: Listeners could hear the words but had no time or cues to process the data; pacing and signposting address this.

items.prompt: In Q&A a hostile attendee asks a question built on a false premise. Criteria: keep your credibility, avoid escalation, serve the rest of the audience. Which response is best?

options.label: Correct the premise with one fact, address the underlying concern, and offer to continue afterwards
Ignore the premise and answer a different, easier question so the exchange ends without any conflict
Tell the questioner they are wrong and ask them to move on, so the remaining audience stays on schedule
Accept the premise as stated to keep the peace, then adjust the rest of your talk to fit that premise

items.explanation: A brief factual correction plus answering the real concern protects credibility and avoids escalation.

items.prompt: Midway through a 10-minute pitch, the organiser signals that you have 3 minutes left, but 5 minutes of content remain, including your ask. Criteria: the ask must land, the audience keeps clarity, your credibility stays intact. What is the best move?

options.label: Drop the ask and finish the details, since the audience can request the recommendation later in writing
Skip the least critical points, mention the cut briefly, and give the ask and a clear close in time
Speed up and cover everything, since skipping any content would make you look unprepared to the audience
Stop and ask the organiser for extra time, since the ask needs the full five minutes to be understood

items.explanation: When time runs short, cutting the least important points lets you still make your ask and close clearly, so the audience leaves knowing what you need.

items.prompt: A speaker plans to answer every Q&A question with total confidence and never say 'I don't know'. Which are well-founded critiques of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bridging away from questions to prepared points can read as evasive and erode trust with the questioner.
Confidence comes entirely from vocal volume, so the real weakness is that the speaker has not practised speaking louder.
An invented answer that is later checked costs more credibility than a brief honest limit would have.
Audiences always punish any admission of ignorance, so the plan is correct but should be applied more forcefully.

items.explanation: Fabrication and evasion both damage trust; a bounded honest answer with follow-up is stronger.

items.prompt: You will give a 15-minute talk, with no interpreter, to an audience where half are non-native English speakers. Which design elements meet this constraint? Select all that apply.

options.label: Read the slide text aloud quickly so listeners hear and see the same words, which saves explanation time.
Pack the slides with jargon, so every listener recognises the field's vocabulary and sees your expertise.
Pair each key term with a simple visual and repeat it consistently rather than using synonyms.
Use short sentences at a slightly slower pace and avoid idioms.

items.explanation: Plain structure, pacing and consistent terms with visuals aid comprehension.

items.prompt: A proposed design for a persuasive talk to a sceptical board has a hook, three claims with evidence, a story and a closing ask. The goal is board approval. What is the design most clearly missing?

options.label: A second story, because boards approve on emotion, so more narrative would make up for any weakness in the evidence.
A longer agenda slide, because a detailed roadmap is what makes a board trust the speaker's preparation.
A bigger opening statistic, since the shock value of the first thirty seconds is what decides board approval.
A plan to address the board's most likely objection, so the case does not end up depending on silence about it.

items.explanation: A sceptical board's likely objection must be handled openly or the case stays vulnerable.

items.prompt: You will give the same talk twice: once to 12 people in a meeting room, then to 400 in an auditorium with a stage and a screen. Design the adaptation that best fits both settings.

options.label: Keep the room version conversational and interactive; in the auditorium use larger gestures, slower pacing, fewer bolder slides and rehearsed questions.
Keep the room version formal and scripted; in the auditorium move quickly among the audience with a handheld microphone and hold open discussion throughout.
Use identical slides, gestures and pacing for both settings, because a single well-practised version keeps the delivery consistent and reliable anywhere.
Keep the room version brief; in the auditorium put detailed text on dense slides and read them aloud, because large audiences retain written information better.

items.explanation: Scale changes the delivery: intimacy and interaction in a small room, projection and simplicity in a large one.
